subtype: Approach: copying a friend's budget percentages [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Pankaj, and in my first month as an analyst I copied a friend's budget. Vasudha had sent me a video about a fifty-thirty-twenty split: half for needs, thirty for wants, twenty for savings. It looked neat, so I put it in my notes and felt organised. Then the month began. I send a good part of my pay home, and I share a flat with two others, so my rent and bills were far more than half. The wants slice was meaningless. By the tenth I was borrowing from the savings slice to pay for basic things. The rule was fine for someone in a different life. I had never asked whether it fitted mine, and my obligations did not fit inside those three boxes.

qa.q: Which friend sent Pankaj the video about the split?
qa.a: Vasudha sent Pankaj the video about the fifty-thirty-twenty split.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel at the start of the month after copying the rule?
qa.a: Pankaj felt organised and pleased at first, before finding that the split did not fit real life.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do instead of copying a rule, and why?
qa.a: Pankaj could begin with the money sent home and the shared rent and see what remains, because the plan then reflects real duties.

qa.q: How might the people at home see the money Pankaj sends?
qa.a: The people at home probably rely on the money and may worry if it were cut to fit a rule that ignores them.

grounding: An analyst copies a popular percentage split from a video without noticing money sent home and shared housing make it unrealistic.

subtype: Approach: copying a friend's budget percentages [Pitfall]
passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday. Kavitha, employee wellbeing desk.
Lakshmi, an analyst in her first year, came in upset. She has been following a 50-30-20 split from a video her friend shared: half for needs, thirty percent for wants, twenty for savings. 'It's the rule everyone uses,' she said.
Her month doesn't fit it. She sends ₹10,000 home to her parents every month, and her share of the flat, with deposit instalments, takes another ₹11,000. On ₹34,000, that alone is more than half. To keep the 'twenty percent savings', she had been skipping meals and borrowing from a flatmate.
She kept apologising, as if she had failed the rule. I told her the rule had failed her month.
We agreed she will list her real obligations first. I have also booked her into the company's free financial counselling session next Tuesday.

qa.q: How much does Lakshmi send home every month?
qa.a: ₹10,000 home to her parents every month.
She feels ashamed, as if failing the borrowed rule means she has failed, although her obligations made it impossible.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Lakshmi's month better than the borrowed split?
qa.a: Starting from her real obligations, the money home and the flat, then planning what is left, with the counselling session to guide her.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi's situation look to the counsellor who wrote the note?
qa.a: The counsellor sees a careful analyst blaming herself and reframes it: the rule never fit her month, so the plan must start from her own duties.

grounding: Shows a young analyst copying a popular percentage rule that ignores money sent home and shared housing, so the split fails.

subtype: Approach: copying a friend's budget percentages [Pitfall]
passage:
Tuesday, 11:40 p.m. Pallavi, you absolute planner.
Zeenat's budget looked so clean when she showed me: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings, colour-coded. She says a video taught her. She lives at home with her parents, though. No rent.
I copied it exactly on the 1st. Tonight I checked. My salary is ₹26,000. My room share is ₹9,500, in a PG with three other girls. Then ₹5,000 to Amma for my brother's school fees, which I promised before I even got the job. Add phone and bus pass and needs came to 61% before groceries.
So to hit the '20% savings', I've been eating biscuits for dinner, and I cancelled going home for Pongal. That's not saving, that's pretending.
Tomorrow: new sheet. Amma's money and the rent at the top, because they're not optional. Whatever's left, I'll split after. Zeenat's version can stay hers.

qa.q: How does Pallavi feel about the copied budget by the end of the entry?
qa.a: Frustrated and a little ashamed of pretending, but determined, with a new sheet planned that puts the rent and Amma's money first.

qa.q: What would you change first in Pallavi's plan?
qa.a: Put the fixed promises, the rent and the money for Amma, at the top and plan the rest after, rather than squeezing meals and trips home to fit a borrowed split.

qa.q: Why might Zeenat's version work for Zeenat but not for Pallavi?
qa.a: Zeenat lives at home with no rent, so needs take a smaller share; the same split cannot hold Pallavi's rent and the promise to Amma.

grounding: Shows a young earner copying a friend's percentage budget and finding that rent and money for family make it unrealistic.
